children: Iron ore prices fell for a third straight session on Friday and were heading for their first weekly loss in three, pressured by lower-than-anticipated demand and a sharp squeeze in steel margins in top consumer China.
The most-traded iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
slid 1.98% to 716.5 yuan ($106.77) a metric ton, as of 0145 GMT, its lowest level since September 3. It has lost 1.4% so far this week, the biggest weekly decline since late July.

The benchmark October iron ore (SZZFV6) on the Singapore Exchange slipped 1.21% to $97 a ton, as of 0135 GMT after earlier hitting the lowest since August 24 at $96.8, a decline of 2.6% so far this week, the biggest weekly fall in nearly three months.
Demand for the key steelmaking ingredient fell as some steelmakers trimmed steel output amid widening losses, souring investor sentiment.

The average daily hot metal output, a gauge of iron ore demand, dipped by 0.2% from the week before to 2.36 million tons as of September 10, while only around 7.8% of steelmakers are operating at a profit, compared to 30% the week before, data from consultancy Mysteel showed.

"China is unlikely to drive another structural supercycle, while Simandou and other supply growth should constrain prices over time," analysts at BMI said in a note, seeing $80 a ton as increasingly meaningful cost support.
Simandou is an iron ore project in Guinea that is ramping up supply.
Other steelmaking ingredients similarly languished with coking coal
Steel benchmarks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange also lost ground on falling raw materials prices.
